  1. Download Unetbootin and select the distribution you wish to use (Distro: Linux Mint, Version: 17.2_Live_x64 [64 bit] or 17.2_Live [32-bit] in our case) and create a live USB with it.
  2. Restart your system and boot from the USB (Likely need to change the boot order in your BIOS [del] when booting up your pc)
  3. When you boot through the USB choose the UEFI boot option and then just follow the install instructions once you get to the mint desktop.

There is an icon on the live boot desktop that says something like "install now" and it will walk you through the rest. Super simple. Honestly. Make sure you have a wifi signal or ethernet cable for access to the net so you can do a full update once installed. Mint cinnamon flavour might have a bit more heft than other distros but it comes with some things pre installed that a user like yourself would appreciate (libre office and codecs to name a few). Not all dristros do that which can make initial set up for someone just getting into linux a bit overwhelming. Just make sure you have access to the internet when playing in your new environment as the Ubuntu and mint forums area a wealth of knowledge.

Don't pay much attention to this part unless you are going to dual boot windows and linux

Install windows first and then linux if starting with a fresh drive. Windows will overwrite the the MBR and mess everything up (I'm being a little dramatic but it's a bit more of a headache) if you install it after mint. ENSURE that you select the UEFI install for windows and for your flavour of Mint if you're going to dual boot. You can't install one through UEFI and one through the other option (MBR I think).

Don't let the last section scare you away from a dual boot. It's just there as a warning since my last attempt at dual boot ended up taking like 5 hours just to realise a silly little thing I over looked.

On one of the first forums I posted on, starting in about '98, we came to refer to any really blatant intellectual dishonesty - obvious quotes out of context, straw men, non sequiturs, red herrings and the like - as "Brophisms," because there was one poster named Broph who was notable for really blatantly using those sorts of tactics.

Think about that for a moment. That was in a community of at least a few hundred posters, and of course there were other instances of that sort of nonsense, but there was one person who was so notable for using those tactics that his name ended up attached to them.

I'm beginning to suspect that it's an illustration of an actual decrease in rationality, though I can't be sure if that's an actual culture-wide decrease or just a decrease that happened as internet access became more the rule rather than the exception (I hope it's more the latter, but I'm not convinced of that). I don't think that most of these people are overtly dishonest - that they recognize that there might be some inherent flaw in their thinking and are actually trying to avoid facing that. I think that they sincerely don't know how to reason - that they've simply adopted some bit of dogma for whatever reason (generally because holding to that bit of dogma serves some part of the self-image to which they're attached), and they've never actually thought about any of it. There's absolutely no point in wasting time on those people. They cannot be reached. Not only is reason entirely beyond them, but since they've adopted their dogma for wholly personal and generally emotional reasons, they have a vested interest in defending it at all costs. Since there's no fallacy that's beneath them, and since they're emotionally invested in their positions, they quite literally will never even consider any other viewpoint. They really can't without posing a threat to their self-images, and armed as they are with an enormous set of fallacies and absolutely no understanding of actual reason, they don't have to. So they don't, and it makes absolutely no difference what anyone else might ever say to them.

That's an interesting perspective, with all the limits that anecdotal evidence has.

Of course there are a variety of possible explanations.

One is that, as you mention, wider Internet access means that we end up interacting with a, shall we say, less “selected” crowd (not that technical proficiency 20 years ago was any guarantee for rationality, sadly), so that certain cognitive patterns are more visible online, while they were mostly only visible offline before.

Another possibility might be, in fact, a general “dumbing down”, or “lazying up” of the population, so that actually more people today have such a dogmatic and superficial approach.

But there's also another explanation, which might be just a matter of community size: a few hundreds people might have been large for the day, but it's still relatively small. In fact, it's barely noticeable compared to size of some online communities today. And in a smaller community it doesn't take that long to know many if not most of the other members, especially the more prominent ones. So in some sense, in a smaller community it's easier to identify characteristic traits of specific individuals, whereas a larger one is more “anonymous”, in that even when there are nicknames and whatnot, in many cases you don't even realize when you're interacting with the same people and when not. And that alone might be sufficient to prevent the creation of neologisms such as «Brophism»: so even though one ends up coming across “one on every thread, everywhere, all the time”, one doesn't even realize if it's actually just always the same small claque (which is another point: if there's one Broph every few hundred users, there's likely to be tens or even hundreds of Brophs if there are thousands of users, so coming across at least one in a thread ends up being more likely).
